title: Half treble
subtitle: UK half treble equals US half double crochet — the compromise stitch between dc and treble
excerpt: Half treble sits between double crochet and treble in height. Denser than treble, taller than double crochet, with a soft drape that suits scarves, baby blankets, and beanies. UK "htr" equals US "hdc" — both spell out as "half double crochet" in US convention.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet stitch chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet, half-treble demonstrations across the late-Victorian volumes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The horizontal bar that sits behind the top V of a half treble stitch. Working into this third loop instead of the top V creates a distinctive ridged texture used in decorative variations.

heroPrompt: A small swatch of half treble in cream DK cotton, six rows worked, plain pale background, soft daylight — the stitches sit slightly taller than double crochet with a soft drape and a distinctive horizontal bar at the back of each stitch top.

content.text: Half treble sits between double crochet and treble in height. About 7 mm tall in DK cotton at 4 mm hook tension — taller than dc, shorter than tr. The fabric is denser than treble (no gaps to see daylight through), with more drape than double crochet. The compromise stitch, and the one most baby-blanket patterns reach for first.
UK half treble equals US half double crochet. The UK abbreviation is "htr"; the US abbreviation is "hdc". The move is identical — three loops on the hook, all pulled through together at the end.

attrs.title: What you need for a learning swatch
attrs.body: 20 g of plain DK-weight cotton in a light colour. A 4 mm hook. A tapestry needle and scissors. Cotton again — wool stretches when you tug, which makes early swatches harder to read.

content.text: Half treble uses a 2-chain turning chain that does not count as a stitch. Start with a slip knot. Chain 12 (ten chains for a 10-stitch row, plus two for the turning chain).

Row 1: yarn over (this is the start of the stitch). Insert the hook into the third chain from the hook (skip 2 chains for the turning chain). Yarn over again, pull a loop back through the chain. Three loops on the hook. Yarn over once more and pull through all three loops at once. One loop remains on the hook — the first half treble is finished.
Work one half treble in each of the next 9 chains. You now have 10 half trebles in the row.
Row 2 and on: turn the work. Ch 2 (does not count as a stitch). Yarn over. Work 1 htr in the first stitch (the very same stitch the hook is in). Work 1 htr in each of the next 9 stitches. (10 sts.)
Repeat row 2 for as many rows as you want. Six rows shows the texture clearly. Fasten off; sew in the tails.

Half treble follows the same four-beat sequence as treble and double treble — yarn over, insert hook, yarn over and pull through, yarn over and pull through ALL loops. The difference is the final pull-through. Double crochet pulls through two loops twice. Half treble pulls through three loops once. Treble pulls through two loops twice, but starts with one extra yarn-over. Same building block, three different stitches.

attrs.heading: When the swatch doesn't look right
attrs.intro: Three common half treble problems and the fix for each.

items.symptom: The swatch grows wider row by row
items.cause: You worked an extra htr at the end of the row — into the previous turning chain, which on UK half treble does NOT count as a stitch.
items.fix: The last htr of each row goes into the last actual stitch. The 2-chain turning chain at the start of the previous row is not a stitch; don't work into it.

items.symptom: The swatch grows narrower row by row
items.cause: You skipped the first stitch (treating the 2-chain turning chain as a stitch).
items.fix: The 2-chain turning chain does NOT count. After turning and chaining 2, work the first htr directly into the first stitch. Count to 10 at the end of every row.

items.symptom: The right edge has a tall thin loop sticking up
items.cause: The 2-chain turning chain stays visible as a thin spike if the next row's first stitch doesn't anchor it down.
items.fix: After turning, yarn over, then go into the first stitch — not into the turning chain itself. The first htr sits beside the turning chain. The chain becomes barely visible once the next row is worked.

content.text: Half treble is the right stitch for a beginner blanket — softer than double crochet, faster than working in trebles, and the fabric drapes well. Once a swatch sits flat and even, try a 60 × 60 cm baby blanket in half treble across the whole width; one ball of DK cotton per stripe makes a self-striping piece without any colour-change instructions to follow.
